items.title: Numerical reasoning: percentage changes in two steps (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: From level 3, most numerical questions need two steps, and the skill is keeping them in order. For a reduction, find the percentage amount and subtract it. For an increase, find the amount and add it. A quick way is a multiplier: a 15% reduction leaves 85% of the price, so multiply by 0.85. A 5% rise gives 105%, so multiply by 1.05. Worked example: a £60 item has 15% off. Ten per cent is £6 and 5% is £3, so 15% is £9, and £60 minus £9 is £51. Using the multiplier gives 60 × 0.85 = 51. VAT works the same way. VAT at 20% on £15 adds £3, making £18. To find a percentage change, divide the change by the original and multiply by 100: rent rising from £600 to £660 is a £60 change, and 60 ÷ 600 = 0.1, which is 10%. When a question takes a percentage of a percentage, multiply the proportions: half of the 40% who work part-time is 20% of everybody. Write down each step, and check that your answer is in the right direction, smaller for a reduction and larger for an increase.

questions.prompt: A £60 item is reduced by 15% in a sale. What is the sale price?
A salary of £28,000 rises by 5%. What is the new salary?
An item costs £15 before VAT. VAT is charged at 20%. What is the price including VAT?
A team of 80 has 15% absent. How many are at work?
Monthly rent rises from £600 to £660. What is the percentage increase?
questions.hint: The rise is £60; 60 ÷ 600 = 0.1, which is 10%.

questions.prompt: In a department, 40% of staff work part-time, and half of the part-time staff are women. What percentage of all staff are part-time women?
questions.hint: Half of 40% is 20%.

questions.prompt: Two-fifths of a 150-strong workforce is based in London. How many are not based in London?
A laptop's price falls from £180 to £153. What is the percentage reduction?
questions.hint: The fall is £27; 27 ÷ 180 = 0.15, which is 15%.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: averages, ratios and rates in two steps (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Averages, ratios and rates become two-step problems at this level. If you know the mean and how many values there are, you can find the total by multiplying: a mean of 14 across five numbers means a total of 70. Take away the totals you know, and what is left is the missing value. For a ratio, add the parts, divide the amount by that total to find one part, then multiply by the part you want. Worked example: £360 is shared in the ratio 5:4. There are 9 parts, one part is £40, and the larger share is 5 × 40 = £200. If you know one part, you can work back: if the larger team of a 3:7 split has 28 people, one part is 4, and the whole is 10 parts, so 40 people. For a rate such as speed, use distance divided by time. 150 miles in 3 hours is 50 miles per hour. The median of an even number of values is halfway between the two middle values once they are in order. For work problems, multiply people by hours to get the total effort, then divide by the new number of people. Check that your answer is reasonable.

questions.prompt: The mean of five numbers is 14. Four of them are 10, 12, 15 and 18. What is the fifth number?
£360 is shared between two people in the ratio 5:4. How much is the larger share?
Cement and sand are mixed in the ratio 3:5 to make 40 kg of mix. How much sand is in the mix?

options.text: 25 kg
15 kg
5 kg
8 kg

questions.hint: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 kg per part; 5 × 5 = 25 kg.

questions.prompt: Two teams are in the ratio 3:7. The larger team has 28 people. How many people are there in both teams?
questions.hint: 28 ÷ 7 = 4 per part; 10 parts × 4 = 40.

questions.prompt: A van travels 150 miles in 3 hours. What is its average speed?

options.text: 450 mph
53 mph
50 mph
0.02 mph

questions.hint: Speed = distance ÷ time = 150 ÷ 3 = 50 mph.

questions.prompt: Four callers waited 2, 3, 5 and 10 minutes. What was the mean waiting time?

options.text: 20 minutes
4 minutes
10 minutes
5 minutes

questions.hint: Total is 20; 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20?
questions.hint: The two middle values are 8 and 10; halfway between them is 9.

questions.prompt: Three staff take 12 hours to complete a task. How long would four staff take, working at the same speed?

options.text: 16 hours
9 hours
11 hours
15 hours

questions.hint: Total effort is 3 × 12 = 36 hours; 36 ÷ 4 = 9.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: pay, fares and conversions in two steps (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Practical money questions at this level combine two operations. Read the question slowly and decide the order. For pay, multiply the hours by the rate, and be careful about whether the question asks for a day, a week or a month. For a fare where a return costs double a single, work out the return first and then multiply by the number of travellers. For a charge made up of a rate and a fixed fee, calculate the variable part and then add the fee: a parcel of 2.5 kg at £1.20 a kilogram plus £3 handling costs 2.5 × 1.20 = £3, plus £3, which is £6. To convert to another currency, multiply or divide by the rate. If £1 buys €1.20, then €96 is worth 96 ÷ 1.20 = £80. For car park charges that include a first-hour fee, apply the first-hour price once and the extra price for the remaining hours only. Fuel questions use a rate such as miles per gallon: divide the distance by the rate to find the amount used. Combine units carefully; convert kilometres and metres to the same unit before adding. Set your work out in clear steps and re-read the question to make sure you answered what was asked.

questions.prompt: An employee earns £9.50 an hour and works 8 hours a day for 5 days. What is her pay for the week?
A single train fare is £14.50 and a return costs double. What is the cost of 3 return tickets?
A car does 40 miles to the gallon. How many gallons are needed for a 120-mile journey?

options.text: 4,800 gallons
80 gallons
0.33 gallons
3 gallons

questions.prompt: A route is 3.2 km long and a second route is 450 m long. What is the total length of the two routes in metres?
A meeting runs from 13:45 to 16:20, including a 30-minute break. How long was the working time?

options.text: 2 hours 35 minutes
3 hours 5 minutes
2 hours 25 minutes
2 hours 5 minutes

questions.hint: 13:45 to 16:20 is 2 h 35 min; subtract 30 min to get 2 h 5 min.

questions.prompt: A courier charges £1.20 a kilogram plus £3 handling. What is the cost of sending a 2.5 kg parcel?
The rate is €1.20 to £1. A hotel costs €96 a night. What is the cost of 3 nights in pounds?
A car park charges £2.50 for the first hour and £1.50 for each extra hour. What is the cost of parking for 4 hours?
questions.hint: First hour £2.50 plus 3 extra hours at £1.50 = £4.50; total £7.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: short data tables in the question (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Level 3 questions put a few figures into the question and ask you to analyse them. Take a moment to list the data in a tidy way, such as a mini table on your scrap paper. Decide what the question asks: a percentage increase, a share of the total, a mean, or the one with the biggest change. Worked example: applications were 120 in January, 150 in February and 180 in March. The increase from January to March is 60, and 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5, so it is a 50% rise. Share of a total: if three departments have sales of £4,000, £3,000 and £3,000, then the total is £10,000 and the first department's share is 4,000 ÷ 10,000 = 40%. For 'which period saw the biggest increase', compare the change from one period to the next, not the totals. The highest total is not always the biggest rise. For a target, add up what has been done and subtract from the target to see what is left. If answers are given as fractions, simplify them: 10 out of 60 is one sixth. Always check you have used the right figures from the question, and whether it uses totals or changes.

questions.prompt: Applications received were 120 in January, 150 in February and 180 in March. What was the percentage increase from January to March?
questions.hint: The rise is 60; 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5, which is 50%.

questions.prompt: Three departments recorded sales of £4,000, £3,000 and £3,000. What percentage of the total was recorded by the first department?
Of 60 complaints, 30 were about delays, 20 about rudeness and 10 about errors. What fraction were about errors?

options.text: One third
One tenth
One fifth
One sixth

questions.hint: 10 out of 60 simplifies to 1/6.

questions.prompt: Daily reports filed on Monday to Friday were 14, 18, 16, 20 and 12. What was the mean number a day?
Quarterly sales were 200, 270, 300 and 330 in Quarters 1 to 4. Which quarter had the biggest increase on the quarter before?

options.text: Quarter 2 (up 70)
Quarter 4 (highest total, 330)
Quarter 3 (up 30)
Quarter 1 (lowest total, 200)

questions.hint: Rises: Q2 +70, Q3 +30, Q4 +30, so Q2 was the biggest.

questions.prompt: A target is 500 cases. So far Team A has closed 180, Team B 140 and Team C 95. How many more cases are needed to reach the target?
questions.hint: Closed so far 415; 500 − 415 = 85.

questions.prompt: In a survey of 400 people, 45% were satisfied and 35% were neutral. The rest were dissatisfied. How many were dissatisfied?
Offices A, B and C have 12, 18 and 30 staff. What is the ratio of Office A staff to Office C staff in its simplest form?
questions.hint: 12:30 divides by 6 to give 2:5.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: speed, distance, time and scale (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Distance, speed and time questions follow one triangle of facts. Distance equals speed multiplied by time. Speed equals distance divided by time. Time equals distance divided by speed. Make sure your units match: if speed is in miles per hour, time must be in hours. A time of 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours. Worked example: a car travelling at 60 mph for 2.5 hours covers 60 × 2.5 = 150 miles. A journey of 90 miles at 45 mph takes 90 ÷ 45 = 2 hours, so leaving at 08:15 you arrive at 10:15. Rates also appear in other settings: a printer making 30 pages a minute needs 450 ÷ 30 = 15 minutes for a 450-page job. For work shared between people, multiply people by time to get the total effort. For scale maps, if 1 cm on the map stands for 5 km, then 6.5 cm stands for 6.5 × 5 = 32.5 km. Questions about take-home pay deduct a percentage from the total: find the percentage amount, then subtract. Draw a quick note of what is given and what is asked, and check that the answer has the right unit.

questions.prompt: A car travels at 60 mph for 2.5 hours. How far does it go?

options.text: 24 miles
150 miles
62.5 miles
120 miles

questions.hint: Distance = 60 × 2.5 = 150 miles.

questions.prompt: Three staff can finish a job in 8 hours. How long would it take six staff working at the same pace?

options.text: 16 hours
8 hours
2 hours
4 hours

questions.hint: Total effort is 24 hours; 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

questions.prompt: A printer makes 30 pages a minute. How long does a 450-page document take?

options.text: 13,500 minutes
480 minutes
7.5 minutes
15 minutes

questions.hint: 450 ÷ 30 = 15 minutes.

questions.prompt: A 90-mile journey is made at an average of 45 mph, leaving at 08:15. What time does the traveller arrive?
A machine scans 30 forms an hour. How many forms does it scan in 4.5 hours?
Fuel costs £1.45 a litre. What is the cost of 40 litres?
An agency worker works 7 hours a day for 4 days at £13 an hour and pays 20% in deductions. What is the take-home pay?
On a map, 1 cm stands for 5 km. Two towns are 6.5 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they?

options.text: 1.3 km
325 km

items.title: Verbal reasoning: true, false or cannot say, longer workplace passages (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: At level 3 the passages have three or four sentences, and the statement may depend on putting two facts together. You still use only the passage. A helpful routine is to read the passage, number the facts in the margin, and then read the statement and decide which numbers it uses. A statement can be True because two facts combine: if 'the office has 50 desks' and 'a fifth are reserved', then 'ten desks are reserved' is True. A statement is False when it clashes with any fact, even a small one. It is Cannot say when it needs information that is missing, or when it states a reason or opinion that is not in the text. Watch for words that change strength: 'may' is weaker than 'will', 'some' is weaker than 'most', and 'all' is stronger than 'most'. Also watch for time words, such as 'currently', 'last year' or 'by next month'. Worked example: 'Overtime is paid at time and a half for hours above 37.' The statement 'Anyone working 40 hours gets overtime for 3 hours' is True. 'Everyone is paid more at weekends' is Cannot say. Do not let general knowledge decide.

questions.prompt: "The office has 50 desks. A fifth of them are reserved for visitors and the rest are shared between staff. Staff may book a shared desk up to a week ahead." Statement: "Ten desks are reserved for visitors." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: forty desks are reserved for visitors
True: a fifth of 50 desks is ten
Cannot say: the passage does not say which visitors
Cannot say: the passage does not give the booking times

questions.hint: One fifth of 50 is 10.

questions.prompt: "Overtime is paid at time and a half for hours worked above 37 in a week. Overtime must be approved by a line manager before it is worked." Statement: "Approved overtime is paid at a higher rate than normal hours." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: time and a half is more than the normal rate
False: overtime is paid at the normal rate
Cannot say: the passage does not give the hourly rate
Cannot say: the passage does not say who approves it

questions.hint: Time and a half means 1.5 times the normal rate, which is higher.

questions.prompt: "The department received 1,210 enquiries in March, which is 10% more than in February. Most enquiries were about benefits, and the rest were about housing." Statement: "The department received 1,100 enquiries in February." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: False: 10% less than 1,210 is 1,089
Cannot say: the passage does not give the February figure
True: 10% more than 1,100 is 1,210
False: February must have been 1,200

questions.hint: 1,100 × 1.1 = 1,210, which matches March.

questions.prompt: "All staff must complete the online security course by 31 March. Staff who have not finished by then will lose access to the shared drive until they do." Statement: "A member of staff who has not completed the course by 31 March will permanently lose access." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: staff must complete the course by 31 March
Cannot say: the passage does not say how long the course is
False: access is lost only until the course is done
Cannot say: the passage does not name the shared drive

questions.hint: The passage says access is lost until they finish, so it is not permanent.

questions.prompt: "The support team handled 450 calls last week. Eighty per cent were answered within two minutes. The longest wait was eleven minutes." Statement: "At least 360 calls were answered within two minutes." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: 80% of 450 calls is 360
False: only 90 calls were answered in two minutes
Cannot say: the passage does not say how many calls there were
Cannot say: wait times vary through the week

questions.prompt: "Because of building work, the north entrance will be closed for two weeks from Monday. Staff are asked to use the south entrance, which has a slower security check." Statement: "The north entrance will reopen in two weeks." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: False: it will remain closed after the building work
Cannot say: the passage does not give the date of the work
True: it is closed for two weeks from Monday
Cannot say: the passage does not say who is doing the work

questions.hint: Two weeks from Monday means it reopens after that period.

questions.prompt: "The training budget has been reduced by 10% this year. Managers should prioritise courses that are required by law before other courses." Statement: "Courses required by law will be cancelled." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: the training budget has been reduced
Cannot say: the cost of those courses is not given
False: the passage says they are to be prioritised
Cannot say: the number of courses is not given

questions.hint: Required courses come first, so they will not be cancelled.

questions.prompt: "Customer satisfaction scores rose from 72% to 78% after the new phone system was installed. The system was installed in April." Statement: "The new phone system caused customer satisfaction to improve." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: scores rose after the installation
Cannot say: the passage shows the rise but gives no cause
False: other changes also took place that year
False: scores were already rising for months before April that year

questions.hint: The passage reports a rise that followed the change, but does not say that the system caused it.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: true, false or cannot say, reports and policy (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Policy and report passages are often formal in style. They use longer sentences, passive verbs and careful wording such as 'it is proposed', 'the review found' or 'is expected to'. The same rules apply, but you must read more slowly. Strip the sentence down to who did what. 'The review found that waiting times had fallen' tells you the review found it, not that it is certain. 'It is expected to save £2 million' tells you an expectation, not a fact. Worked example: 'The scheme, which is expected to start next year, will give grants to small businesses. Applications will be assessed by a panel.' The statement 'The scheme has started' is False, because it is expected next year. The statement 'The panel will assess applications' is True. The statement 'Grants will be £5,000' is Cannot say. When a passage is about intentions or proposals, a statement written as a certainty is rarely True. When a passage is about results and the statement claims a reason, check whether the reason is given. Taking an extra moment to translate the formal wording into simple words can make the answer clear.

questions.prompt: "The scheme, which is expected to start next year, will give grants to small businesses. Applications will be assessed by an independent panel." Statement: "The scheme has already started." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: the scheme gives grants to businesses
Cannot say: the passage does not say how large the grants are
Cannot say: the passage does not name the panel members
False: it is only expected to start next year

questions.hint: 'Expected to start next year' means it has not begun.

questions.prompt: "A review of the licensing process found that applications took an average of 12 weeks to decide. The review recommends reducing this to 8 weeks." Statement: "The review recommends that applications are decided in 8 weeks." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: the review says 12 weeks is acceptable
Cannot say: the review does not say how it will be done
True: the review recommends reducing the time to 8 weeks
Cannot say: the review does not say who made the request

questions.hint: The passage states the recommended target as 8 weeks.

questions.prompt: "It is proposed that the opening hours of the contact centre be extended from 6pm to 8pm on weekdays. A decision will be made after consultation." Statement: "The contact centre will open until 8pm on weekdays." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: opening hours will be extended to 8pm
Cannot say: the extension is only a proposal pending consultation
False: the centre will close at 6pm
False: the centre will open until 8pm on weekends rather than weekdays

questions.hint: A proposal that awaits a decision has not been confirmed.

questions.prompt: "The report found that 65% of staff felt well supported by their managers, up from 58% two years ago. It also found that staff in smaller teams were more positive." Statement: "Support from managers was rated higher than two years ago." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: the figure rose from 58% to 65%
False: staff in large teams were more positive
Cannot say: the passage does not say how many staff replied
Cannot say: the passage does not say why the figure changed

questions.hint: 65% is higher than 58%.

questions.prompt: "The government has announced that new rules on recycling will be introduced in stages over three years. The first stage will apply to larger businesses." Statement: "Small businesses will have to follow the new recycling rules in the first year." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: the rules will apply to all businesses at some point during the plan
False: only larger businesses are covered by the rules
Cannot say: the passage names larger businesses for stage one only
False: the rules start after three years

questions.hint: Stage one is for larger businesses; the timing for small ones is not given.

questions.prompt: "Passengers on the regional rail network increased by 4% last year, although the number of trains stayed the same. Overcrowding complaints also rose." Statement: "The rail network ran more trains last year." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: more passengers used the network
Cannot say: the passage does not give the number of trains
False: the number of trains stayed the same
Cannot say: the passage does not say where the network runs

questions.hint: The passage states that the number of trains was unchanged.

questions.prompt: "The inspection reported that the care home met most national standards. Two areas, record keeping and staff training, were found to need improvement." Statement: "Record keeping at the care home needs improvement." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: False: the home met all of the national standards
Cannot say: the passage does not say how the records were kept
Cannot say: the passage does not name the inspection team
True: it was named as one of the two areas to improve

questions.hint: Record keeping is explicitly listed as needing improvement.

questions.prompt: "The new tax guidance will be published on GOV.UK in the spring. It will replace the leaflets currently sent by post." Statement: "The leaflets sent by post will stop immediately." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: the new guidance replaces the leaflets
Cannot say: the passage gives no date for the leaflets to stop
False: the leaflets will continue to be sent by post for ever more
False: the guidance will be sent by post

questions.hint: The guidance will replace the leaflets, but the start date is not given.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: which conclusion is supported by the passage (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: At this level you may be given a paragraph and four possible conclusions. Only one is firmly supported by the paragraph. The skill is to separate what the text says from what is simply plausible. Work through the options one at a time. Mark each as supported, contradicted or not covered. A conclusion that is supported can be proved using a sentence in the passage, perhaps with simple arithmetic. A contradicted option clashes with a sentence in the passage. A not-covered option adds information, makes a prediction or gives a reason that the text never mentions. Worked example: 'A council cut opening hours at its libraries, and visits fell by 15% in the following year.' The conclusion 'Visits fell after the opening hours were cut' is supported. The conclusion 'Cutting hours caused visits to fall' is not covered, because the passage does not claim a cause. 'Visits will keep falling' is a prediction. Strong words like 'proves', 'always' or 'every' are red flags. If two options seem right, look for the one that stays closest to the passage. Do not choose an option just because it sounds sensible.

questions.prompt: A council cut library opening hours, and visits fell by 15% in the following year. Which conclusion is supported by the passage?

options.text: Cutting the hours was the cause of the fall in visits
Visits fell in the year after the hours were cut
Visits will keep falling every year
Most library users are older people

questions.hint: The passage reports a fall that followed the change, but gives no cause.

questions.prompt: A department received 800 applications for 40 posts. Half of the applicants were rejected at the first stage. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: About 400 applicants went through the first stage
About 40 applicants were rejected
Most applicants were successful
Each of the 40 posts attracted about 10 applicants

questions.hint: Half of 800 is 400, so 400 went on to the next stage.

questions.prompt: Staff survey results showed that 80% of employees felt valued, compared with 70% the year before. The survey was completed by 900 staff. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: A greater share of staff felt valued than the year before
900 staff felt valued
Staff are happier this year because of the recent pay rise
Fewer than 70% of staff responded

questions.hint: 80% is higher than 70%.

questions.prompt: The helpline answers calls from 8am to 8pm. Last month it received 6,000 calls, and 30% of them came after 6pm. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: About 600 calls were received after 6pm
About 1,800 calls were received after 6pm
Most of the calls came in during the evening
The helpline closes at 6pm

questions.prompt: Two reports looked at delays on the road network. The first found delays rose by 5%. The second found delays had not changed but covered only major roads. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: Delays are rising on all types of road across the network
Delays have fallen on major roads
Both reports covered the same roads
The two reports reached different findings on delays

questions.hint: One report found a rise and the other found no change, so they differ.

questions.prompt: Before the new system, forms took 10 days to process. Now they take 6 days on average. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: Forms are processed twice as fast
Forms are processed 4 days faster on average
The new system costs less to run than the old one
Every form is now processed in 6 days

questions.hint: 10 − 6 = 4 days faster; 'on average' rules out the last option.

questions.prompt: Three in every five staff at the centre use public transport to travel to work. There are 200 staff at the centre. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: 60 staff use public transport
3 staff in each team use public transport
120 staff use public transport
Public transport use is falling

questions.prompt: A report on staff turnover found that most leavers cited pay as their main reason. A smaller number cited career development. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: Career development was the main reason given by leavers
Pay was the most common reason given for leaving
Every leaver cited pay
Pay will be increased next year

questions.hint: 'Most' gave pay as the main reason.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: statements that do not follow (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Sometimes the question asks which statement is NOT supported by the passage, or which cannot be concluded. This changes your task: three options are supported and one is not. Read the question stem carefully, because mistaking 'not supported' for 'supported' is one of the commonest errors. Method: check each option against the passage and label it S for supported or N for not supported. The odd one out is your answer. An option can be N for two reasons: it contradicts the text, or it goes beyond the text. Both count. Worked example: 'The depot has 24 vans. A third are electric and the rest are diesel.' Supported: 'Eight vans are electric', 'Sixteen vans are diesel', and 'The depot has more diesel vans than electric vans'. Not supported: 'The electric vans were bought last year'. Because the question asks for the one NOT supported, the last is the answer. It helps to underline NOT in the question as you read it. After choosing, reread the stem once more to confirm that you answered the question that was asked, since in the middle of a test it is easy to forget which kind of question it is.

questions.prompt: The depot has 24 vans. A third are electric and the rest are diesel. Which statement is NOT supported by the passage?

options.text: The electric vans were bought last year
Eight vans are electric
Sixteen vans are diesel
There are more diesel than electric vans

questions.hint: The passage never says when the electric vans were bought.

questions.prompt: The office has 60 staff. Two thirds work in the main building and the others work at the annex. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: Forty staff work in the main building
Twenty staff work at the annex
More staff work in the main building than at the annex
The annex is newer than the main building

questions.hint: Nothing is said about the age of either building.

questions.prompt: Of the 500 letters sent last month, 20% were returned undelivered. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: Most of the returned letters had a wrong postcode
100 letters were returned undelivered
400 letters were delivered
Fewer than half of all the letters were returned undelivered

questions.hint: The passage does not give a reason for the returns.

questions.prompt: A training course runs for three days. Day one covers safety, day two covers customer service and day three is a test. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: The course is held twice a year
The course lasts three days
Safety is covered on the first day
The final day includes a test

questions.hint: The passage does not say how often the course runs.

questions.prompt: The shop sold 120 items on Saturday, and 80 items on Sunday. It was closed on Monday. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: The shop sold 200 items over the weekend
More items were sold on Saturday than on Sunday
The shop was open on Sunday
The shop is closed on Mondays every week

questions.hint: Only one Monday is mentioned, not a weekly pattern.

questions.prompt: In a survey, 45 of 60 respondents said they would use a new online form. The rest said they would prefer paper. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: Three quarters would use the online form
Fifteen respondents preferred paper
The respondents who preferred paper were mostly older
Most respondents were happy to use the online form that was offered

questions.hint: The passage gives no ages for the respondents.

questions.prompt: The new policy applies to staff who have worked at the department for more than a year. Aisha joined six months ago. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: The policy covers staff with over a year's service
Aisha is not yet covered by the policy
The policy does not apply to new joiners
Aisha will benefit from the policy in a month

questions.hint: Six months of service is below the one-year rule, so a month later she is still not covered.

questions.prompt: Complaints about the service fell from 90 in May to 54 in June. Which statement is NOT supported?

options.text: There were fewer complaints in June than in May
There were 36 fewer complaints in June
June complaints were 60% of May's
The fall was due to better staff training

questions.hint: The passage gives no reason for the fall.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: if-then rules and conditions (level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Many rules at work are conditional: if one thing is true, then something follows. A passage might say 'If a form is signed, it will be processed.' This does not say that every processed form was signed, and it does not say what happens to unsigned forms. It only tells you what happens when the condition is met. A rule with 'only if' is stronger. 'Staff may enter the lab only if they have completed safety training' means that training is required, but it does not promise entry once they have it. Worked example: 'A claim is paid if it arrives by Friday.' A claim arriving on Thursday is paid. A claim arriving on Monday may or may not be paid, because the rule does not cover it. Another: 'Only managers can approve leave.' A person who approved leave is a manager. A manager is not certain to approve any particular request. Test each option by asking, 'Does the rule force this?' If it does not, it is not the answer. Pay attention to direction: A leading to B is different from B leading to A. Write the rule as a short arrow note on your scrap paper and follow it step by step.

questions.prompt: If a form is signed and dated, it will be processed within five days. Mr Khan's form was signed and dated. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Mr Khan's form was already processed on time last week
Unsigned forms are never processed
Mr Khan's form will be processed within five days
Mr Khan signed his form on Monday

questions.hint: The condition is met, so the result follows.

questions.prompt: Staff may enter the laboratory only if they have completed safety training. Lena entered the laboratory. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Lena has completed safety training
Lena works in the laboratory
Lena completed the training last week
Everyone with training can enter

questions.hint: 'Only if' means training is required, so Lena must have done it.

questions.prompt: A claim is paid if it arrives by Friday. Claire's claim arrived on Monday. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Claire's claim will be paid
Claire's claim will not be paid because it arrived late
Claire's claim was sent on Friday
The rule does not say whether Claire's claim is paid

questions.hint: The rule covers claims arriving by Friday only; Monday is not covered.

questions.prompt: If the temperature falls below 16 degrees, the heating comes on. The heating is on. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The temperature is below 16 degrees
It is not certain that the temperature has fallen below 16 degrees
The temperature is 16 degrees exactly
The heating has a fault

questions.hint: The heating might also come on for another reason, such as a timer.

questions.prompt: Only managers can approve leave. Joe approved Sam's leave request. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Sam is a manager
Joe approves all requests
Joe is a manager
Sam's leave was for a week

questions.hint: Only managers can approve, so the approver must be a manager.

questions.prompt: If a visitor signs in at reception, they are given a badge. Priya was given a badge. Which statement is correct?

options.text: We cannot be sure that Priya signed in at reception
Priya must have signed in at the reception desk earlier today
Priya is a member of staff
Priya was not given a badge

questions.hint: The rule works one way, and badges might be given for other reasons.

questions.prompt: All applications received before the closing date are scored. Ben's application was not scored. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Ben's application was rejected
Ben's application was scored low
Ben applied for the wrong job
Ben's application was not received before the closing date

questions.hint: If every early application is scored, an unscored one cannot have been early.

questions.prompt: Employees who work more than 6 hours must take a 30-minute break. Hana worked 7 hours. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Hana must take a 30-minute break
Hana took a 30-minute break
Hana worked through her break
All employees get a 30-minute break

questions.hint: The condition is met by working 7 hours.

items.title: Situational judgement: handling mistakes and being open (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Everyone makes mistakes at work. What the Civil Service looks for is how you respond. The behaviours that matter are honesty, taking responsibility, acting quickly and learning from what happened. At level 3 the situations are less clear cut. Several responses may seem reasonable, and you must pick the most effective one. Ask yourself: Does this response put the customer or the public first? Does it involve the right person? Does it prevent the problem from growing? Does it keep records accurate? A good response usually combines a short immediate action with openness. Worked example: you notice that you sent a customer a letter with the wrong date for their appointment. The most effective response is to contact the customer as soon as possible with the correct date, apologise and tell your manager, so that the cause can be checked. It is not as effective to wait to see whether they call, or to send the correction without telling anyone. Blaming someone else, hiding the error or fixing it quietly all fall short. Choose the answer that protects the customer and is open with your manager.

questions.prompt: You notice that you sent a customer a letter with the wrong appointment date. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Wait to see whether the customer calls about the date
Send a corrected letter and say nothing to your manager
Contact the customer with the correct date, apologise and tell your manager
Ask a colleague to check whether any other letters are wrong before contacting the customer

questions.hint: Protecting the customer and being open with your manager puts things right quickly.

questions.prompt: You realise that you gave a customer incorrect advice about a deadline yesterday. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Wait to see whether the customer asks about the deadline again
Correct it on the system but not tell the customer
Ask a colleague to ring the customer so that you are not blamed for giving the wrong advice
Contact the customer promptly to correct the advice and let your manager know

questions.hint: Telling the customer quickly stops them missing the real deadline.

questions.prompt: Your manager tells you that a form you completed contained an error. You believe the error came from an unclear form. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Argue that it was not your fault until the manager agrees
Correct the error and agree it was entirely your fault
Correct the error, then explain why the form was unclear and suggest an improvement
Ignore the feedback, because the form was unclear

questions.hint: Taking responsibility while giving useful feedback helps everyone learn.

questions.prompt: A new colleague makes an error that affects a customer's payment, and asks you not to tell the manager. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Encourage them to tell the manager, and offer to support them
Agree to keep it secret, because they are new
Tell the whole team about the error so that they can all learn from it
Correct the payment and say nothing to anyone

questions.hint: The customer's payment needs fixing and the manager needs to know, but you can be supportive.

questions.prompt: You have just sent a bulk email and spot a spelling mistake in the subject line. The content is correct. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Do nothing, as nobody is harmed
Let your manager know and consider whether a short correction is needed
Send the same email again without explanation
Delete the email from your sent folder

questions.hint: Telling the manager lets them decide if a correction is worth sending.

questions.prompt: During a quiet week, you find an old task you forgot to complete last month. It has now passed its deadline. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Quietly complete it and not mention the lateness to anyone at all
Delete the task so it does not show as overdue
Wait to see whether anyone asks about it
Complete it now, and explain the delay to your manager

questions.hint: Being open about a late task lets your manager deal with any effect.

questions.prompt: A customer complains that their documents were lost. You find they were misfiled by you last week. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the customer the documents will turn up eventually
Tell the customer that they must have sent them to the wrong office in the first place
Find the documents, return them to the customer, apologise and tell your manager
Refile them and hope the customer does not call again

questions.hint: Honest recovery and apology are the right steps.

questions.prompt: You think a colleague entered a wrong figure into a shared record, but you are not sure. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Correct it yourself immediately without asking
Check the source and ask your colleague politely about the figure
Say nothing, since it is their record
Report it to the senior manager first, without checking the source or asking

questions.hint: Checking and asking first is fair and avoids wrongly changing records.

items.title: Situational judgement: working with colleagues and conflict (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Not every colleague is easy to work with, and situational judgement questions at level 3 explore how you cope with disagreement and pressure. The best behaviours are to stay calm, listen, focus on the task, and go to a manager only when talking directly has not worked or the problem is serious. A good first step is usually a private, polite conversation. Raising a concern about a person in front of others, complaining behind their back or avoiding them are all weaker. If the problem involves bullying, harassment, safety or something illegal, you should not try to resolve it alone but raise it with your manager or the proper channel straight away. Worked example: a colleague regularly leaves their share of a team task to you. A good response is to speak to them privately, describe the problem, and agree who does what. If that fails, you tell your manager. Doing all the work in silence, or telling the rest of the team about them, will not solve it. Remember that you are judged on your behaviour, so choose a response that is respectful, constructive and keeps the work going.

questions.prompt: A colleague regularly leaves their share of a team task to you. What is the most effective first response?

options.text: Tell the rest of the team that they are lazy
Keep doing their share and say nothing
Ask your manager to move you to another team so you no longer work with them
Speak to them privately, explain the impact and agree who does what

questions.hint: A calm private conversation is the best first step.

questions.prompt: A colleague speaks to you in a rude way in front of others. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Reply in the same rude way to show them that it is not acceptable behaviour
Stay calm and speak to them privately afterwards about how it affected you
Ignore them in future
Complain about them to other colleagues

questions.hint: A private, calm conversation can resolve the issue and keeps the team positive.

questions.prompt: A colleague confides that a manager has been shouting at them regularly and making them feel afraid. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them to ignore the manager
Confront the manager yourself on their behalf and tell them to stop immediately
Listen, encourage them to report it and offer to go with them if they want
Keep it to yourself because it was said in confidence

questions.hint: Behaviour of this kind should be reported through the proper channel, and you can support them.

questions.prompt: You and another team member have different ideas about how to complete a task. Your deadlines are close. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Do it your way without telling them
Let them do it their way to avoid arguing
Listen to their idea, explain yours and agree the best approach, asking your manager if you cannot agree
Ask a third colleague to choose whose idea is best

questions.hint: Discussing both ideas and escalating only if needed keeps the work moving.

questions.prompt: A colleague takes credit in a meeting for work you did. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say nothing and let it go
Speak to them privately, and make sure your role is made clear to your manager
Interrupt them in the meeting and call them dishonest in front of everyone at the meeting
Stop sharing work with them and with others

questions.hint: A private discussion and clear communication with the manager are respectful and effective.

questions.prompt: A member of your team has been arriving late every day and others have noticed. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Mention it privately and kindly, and ask if there is anything affecting them
Complain about them to the other team members
Tell the manager without speaking to them
Ignore it, because it is not your job

questions.hint: A private, caring conversation first is respectful and may reveal the reason.

questions.prompt: A colleague jokes that a customer who rang earlier was stupid. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say politely that the customer should be treated respectfully
Laugh along, as everyone has frustrating calls now and then
Report the colleague to the director immediately without speaking to them
Repeat the joke to other colleagues

questions.hint: Calmly challenging disrespectful remarks maintains standards.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues ask you to take sides in a disagreement between them. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Support the colleague you know best
Tell both of them that you do not care
Stay neutral, listen to both and encourage them to talk to each other
Report both of them to HR

questions.hint: Staying fair and encouraging dialogue is the most constructive approach.

items.title: Situational judgement: difficult customers and sensitive situations (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Some customers contact the Civil Service when they are worried, angry or upset. This might be about a payment, a decision or a delay, and the person may take it out on you. Situational judgement tests look for patience, empathy and clarity. The principles are to listen first, show that you understand, stay polite, explain what you can do, and be honest about what you cannot. Never promise something that you cannot deliver. If a customer becomes abusive, you can warn them calmly that you will end the call if it continues, and report the incident. If a customer is in distress or says they are at risk, follow your procedures and get help from your manager straight away. Worked example: a customer shouts that their payment is late and they cannot buy food. The best response is to stay calm, acknowledge their worry, check the facts, explain what will happen and when, and use any emergency help that your procedures allow. It is not effective to argue, to say 'it's not my fault' or to promise a payment date you cannot guarantee. Put the customer's needs first within the rules.

questions.prompt: A customer shouts that their payment is late and they cannot buy food. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them that late payments are very common
Promise the payment will arrive tomorrow
Tell them to call back when they feel calmer
Stay calm, acknowledge their worry, check the facts and explain the next steps

questions.hint: Acknowledging the problem and giving accurate next steps shows empathy and honesty.

questions.prompt: A caller is abusive and swears at you repeatedly after you have asked them to stop. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Swear back so that they understand how it feels
Warn that you will end the call if it continues, then follow procedure and report it
Hang up straight away without saying anything
Keep taking the abuse so that they feel heard

questions.hint: A calm warning followed by procedure protects you and is fair to the caller.

questions.prompt: A customer tells you during a call that they feel they cannot go on. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Reassure them and finish the call quickly
Tell them to contact their doctor tomorrow
Change the subject to their application
Stay on the line, take it seriously and follow the procedure to get help

questions.hint: Safety comes first and you should escalate using the proper process.

questions.prompt: A customer insists on being told the outcome of a decision that has not yet been made. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Guess that the outcome will be positive
Tell them to wait and not ring again
Explain that the decision has not been made and say when you expect it
Say you cannot discuss it

questions.hint: Being honest about the status avoids giving false hope.

questions.prompt: A customer visits the office without an appointment and wants an urgent answer. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Listen, check if you can help or find someone who can, and be clear about options
Tell them to book an appointment and leave
Ask them to wait for several hours in reception
Give them an answer you are not sure of

questions.hint: Trying to help while being clear on options treats the customer well.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you for advice on which benefit they should claim. You are not trained to advise on this. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Suggest the one that seems best for them
Explain what you can do and direct them to official guidance or advisers
Say you are unable to help at all
Tell them to ask a friend

questions.hint: Staying within your role and signposting is the right approach.

questions.prompt: A customer complains that you were unhelpful on the phone last week, but you do not remember them. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say you do not remember and so it cannot be true
Listen carefully, apologise that they had a poor experience and try to resolve it
Tell them that you were busy that day
Pass them to someone else without explaining

questions.hint: Listening and trying to put things right is better than defending yourself.

questions.prompt: A customer is confused by a letter written in complicated language and asks you to explain it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Read the letter to them without comment
Tell them it is clear enough
Ask them to find someone else to read it
Explain the letter in plain English and check that they understand

questions.hint: Plain English and checking understanding help the customer act correctly.

items.title: Situational judgement: change, learning and improving the service (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: The Civil Service often changes how it works: new systems, new rules or new ways of working. Situational judgement questions ask how you respond. Positive behaviours include being open to change, asking questions, learning new skills, helping others and offering ideas through the right route. Negative behaviours include resisting without a reason, ignoring the new process or complaining to others. If you believe the change is a mistake, say so politely to your manager, with reasons and evidence, but still follow the process unless it is unsafe or unlawful. Worked example: a new case system replaces the old spreadsheet and you find it slow. A good response is to attend the training, practise, log the problems you find and report them, while using the system as required. Continuing with the spreadsheet in secret means records are split in two places. When you have an idea to improve how something works, share it with your manager, explain the benefit and be willing to test it. Ask yourself whether the response helps the service, respects the rules and supports colleagues.

questions.prompt: A new case system replaces the old spreadsheet, and you find it slow. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Carry on using the old spreadsheet in secret
Use the new system for some cases and keep the spreadsheet for the others
Tell the team the new system is a waste of time
Use it as required, note the problems and report them to your manager

questions.hint: Following the process while reporting issues helps improve it.

questions.prompt: You are invited to training on a new process but you feel confident with the old process. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Skip it, as you already know your job
Attend, as it will show you what has changed and may help others
Attend but do something else during it
Ask a colleague to take notes

questions.hint: Training helps you to work to the new standard.

questions.prompt: You think of a quicker way to complete a routine task. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Share the idea with your manager and explain the benefits
Start using it right away and tell your manager only if it works
Keep it to yourself so that you stay efficient
Tell colleagues to use it without checking

questions.hint: Suggesting improvements through the right route lets them be tested.

questions.prompt: A colleague is struggling to use the new software and has asked you for help. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Show them the basics and point them towards the guidance
Do the work for them every time they get stuck, so that they can carry on
Tell them to attend the training again
Say you are too busy

questions.hint: Supporting colleagues builds shared skills.

questions.prompt: Your team has been asked to use a new form that you think has an error in the guidance. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Fill in the form the way you think it should be
Tell your manager or the form owner, giving the details of the error
Ignore the guidance and carry on
Wait for someone else to notice the problem and report it themselves in time

questions.hint: Reporting the error to the person responsible helps everyone.

questions.prompt: A manager announces a change that you do not agree with. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give your view with reasons in the right setting, then work to the decision
Refuse to follow the change
Tell your colleagues that the manager is wrong
Say nothing and carry on as before

questions.hint: Constructive challenge is welcome, but decisions must then be followed.

questions.prompt: You make a suggestion for improvement, but your manager says it is not possible this year. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Stop making suggestions
Go over your manager's head and take the idea to a senior leader
Complain to colleagues
Accept the decision and ask if you can raise it again later

questions.hint: Accepting the decision and staying positive keeps the relationship strong.

questions.prompt: You have been given a task that needs a skill you do not have. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Try to work it out quietly and hope for the best
Pass the work to a colleague
Do a simpler task instead and leave this one for later
Tell your manager and ask for training or guidance

questions.hint: Being honest about gaps lets you learn what is needed.
